title: They walk humbly
hook: servants of the Merciful walk gently, and when the ignorant address them, say peace (25:63)

segments.voice: Yesterday, furqan, the criterion, and your line was tell right from wrong. What decision did you finally make? Day four hundred ninety-eight.

Someone cuts in front of you in line and then glares at you as if you'd done it. A stranger online replies to a harmless comment with something cruel. A driver leans on the horn and shouts a word you won't repeat. There's a split second where your whole body gets ready to answer in kind. Near its end, Surah Al-Furqan paints a portrait of a certain kind of person, and the first two strokes of the portrait are about exactly this: how they walk, and what they say when someone is rude to them.

Verse sixty-three. The portrait has a title: 'ibad ar-Rahman, the servants of the Most Merciful. Pickthall calls them the faithful slaves of the Beneficent, "who walk upon the earth modestly, and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace". Walk modestly is yamshuna hawnan. Hawn means ease, lightness, gentleness. Not slinking, not timid. Just walking without swagger, without needing the street to notice you. Then the foolish ones, al-jahilun. In older Arabic, jahl isn't only not knowing things. It's the opposite of hilm, forbearance. A jahil is someone hot-tempered, rash, quick to insult. So the scene is: someone flares up at them. And they answer, salaman. Peace. Commentators read that in more than one way. Some say it means a word of peace, a calm reply that refuses to escalate. Others say it means they speak in a way that keeps them safe from sin: they say something decent and move on. Neither reading makes it weakness. A hadith in Bukhari says the strong person isn't the one who wins at wrestling; the strong one is the one who controls himself when angry. That's the strength in this verse. The portrait goes on for another dozen verses, and we'll walk through more of it. But it begins here, at street level. How you carry your body down the road. And the first thing you say when someone throws something at you. The servants of the Merciful get their name from Him. The gentleness is borrowed.
screen: `'IBAD AR-RAHMAN.` · `HAWN: EASE, GENTLENESS.` · `JAHL: THE OPPOSITE OF FORBEARANCE.` · `THE STRONG ONE CONTROLS ANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse answering rudeness with peace. Sit, and let the breath settle. Remember the last time someone was short with you. Feel how your body got ready to reply. Now replay it, slowly, and let your shoulders drop instead. Picture yourself saying something calm and short. Peace. Okay. Have a good day. Then walking on, lightly. If you pray, you can ask for that ease. The bell holds the time.
They walk humbly. The servants of the Merciful walk on the earth gently, and when the rash speak to them, they answer: peace. Today's word.
Your line: walk gently; say peace. Today, the next time someone is rude to you, in person or online, try one calm short reply, or none, and walk on. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers often read 25:63–77, the portrait of 'ibad ar-Rahman, as a description of good character, and quote verse 63 when teaching how to respond to insults.

fork.setup: someone hot-tempered insults you in the street. you're one of the servants of the Merciful. what do you say?
options: nothing, but glare until they leave.
fork.reveal: they answer: peace. commentators read it as a calm word that refuses to escalate, and keeps the speaker clear of wrong.

original.note: Arabic: gently, with ease; 25:63 says the servants of the Merciful walk hawnan.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble and polite.
what it means: walk without swagger, and when a rash person flares up at you, answer with peace instead of matching them.
what a scholar hears: jahl opposed to hilm in pre-Islamic usage; salaman read either as a greeting of disengagement or as speech that keeps one safe from sin; the portrait runs 25:63–77.
